title: Mashed Potatoes with Milk and Gravy

content.title: About
content.content: Mashed potatoes made from fresh potatoes, prepared with milk and gravy, are a smooth, creamy side dish. The potatoes are boiled until tender, then mashed with milk for a silky texture, while the gravy adds a flavorful, slightly thick sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed root vegetables; in 2020 global production exceeded 370 million tonnes.
The tradition of making mashed potatoes with milk began in Europe in the 19th century when milk became more widely available.
Gravy for mashed potatoes is often made from meat stock, but vegetarian versions using vegetable broth are common.
Mashed potatoes are a classic accompaniment to roasted meat, fish, and poultry.
There are many variations: with butter, cheese, garlic, or herbs.

items.title: Rich source of potassium
items.content: Potatoes provide potassium, which supports normal blood pressure and muscle function.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, which helps boost immunity and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates for energy
items.content: The carbs in mashed potatoes supply sustained energy.

items.title: Calcium from milk
items.content: Milk adds calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Low fat when made with skim milk
items.content: Using low‑fat milk keeps the dish relatively low in calories.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so those with diabetes should watch portion size.

items.title: Sodium in gravy
items.content: Prepared gravies can be salty; low‑sodium versions are recommended.

items.title: Bacterial growth if improperly stored
items.content: Leaving mashed potatoes at room temperature for long periods can promote bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the mash hot as a side to meat, fish, or vegetable dishes. Top with fried onions, fresh herbs, grated cheese, or a pat of butter. For a lighter version, use skim milk and reduce the amount of gravy.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the mash to room temperature, then place it in an airtight container and refrigerate for up to 3 days. When reheating, add a splash of milk to restore creaminess. It can be frozen for up to 2 months, though texture may become slightly grainy.
